images.text:
Fingerprinting

Fingerprinting has been one of the most sophisticated techniques used to screen for, discriminate between and identify guilty persons. However, this technique is not new. It was known thousands of years ago. The first people to use fingerprints for identification were the ancient Assyrians and Chinese, who used fingerprints to sign important documents.

The first modern study of fingerprints was made by Johannes Purkinje, a Czech physiologist. Sir Francis Galton, a British scientist, developed his own system of classifying fingerprints using all ten fingers and ascribing them to their “owners”. Sir Francis' system is the basis of the screening system used today.

The first practical use of fingerprints to identify criminals was in Bengal, India, in the 1890s. This was developed by Sir Edward Richard Henry, a police official. In 1901 he screamed with delight when he created the world's first database of fingerprints.

Today, the use of fingerprints is prescribed around the world. Whenever a person touches any hard, smooth object, a fingerprint made by the oil in the skin is left as if the person had made an inscription on the surface. These prints, which cannot be seen by the naked eye, can be detected using powder or special lights. Police are trained to discover fingerprints on almost any surface. These prints are invaluable in the detection and capture of criminals.

Consonant blends are sounds that consist of two or more consonants. They are said together. Sometimes, this can be quite challenging for non-native speakers.

The consonant blend /scr/ consists of three sounds that are said one right after the next.

/s/ + /k/ + /r/

Say each of these sounds out loud.
Then, say them one right after the next.
Concentrate on what your tongue, teeth and lips are doing.

screen
scream
discriminate
ascribe
inscription
prescribe
